content: The effects, costs, and economic impact of assistive technology are critical areas of research. There is limited evidence regarding how assistive technology improves quality of life and its associated societal benefits, including economic advantages such as reducing the number of individuals living with disabilities. While the benefits may seem obvious in individual cases, population-level data is lacking. This evidence is essential to encourage countries to develop or enhance policies and systems for providing assistive products. Key research questions include: What is the return on investment for assistive technology? How does it impact the quality of life for individuals with disabilities? What are the costs of providing assistive technology relative to the outcomes? What are the consequences of not providing assistive technology or providing it inadequately? What is the impact of the most needed assistive products, and which are the most cost-effective? Assistive technology policies, systems, service provision models, and best practices are also under-researched. Many countries lack relevant policies and systems entirely, and there is insufficient knowledge about which approaches are most effective and efficient. Evidence of good practices and suitable approaches in specific contexts is necessary for countries to develop or improve their policies and service provision systems. Developing quality standards can significantly assist government agencies and service providers in enhancing the impact of their assistive technology policies and procedures. Research questions in this area include: What should be the key components of a framework for national assistive technology policy? Which service provision models currently exist, and what is known about their quality, impacts, and outcomes? What constitutes good quality assistive technology service provision, and what are the best practices in this field? How can these best practices be used to develop quality standards and guidelines? How can information about service provision models and best practices be disseminated to implementers and other stakeholders? How can the role of end-users be maximized in the service provision process, including in the design, implementation, and leadership of services? The availability of high-quality and affordable assistive technology is vital to the goals of the GATE initiative. High-income countries tend to focus on high-tech solutions with optimal functionality, while middleand low-income countries require more affordable, accessible, and robust products and services. However, most research and innovation are directed toward high-tech, costly products, with little attention given to developing robust, affordable, and high-quality assistive products that are in greater demand. This disparity is creating an assistive technology divide, similar to the digital divide, where new technologies are rapidly developed, but the majority of the world does not benefit from them. Research questions include: What types of assistive products are most needed, and which have demonstrated the greatest benefit to users? How can high-quality assistive products be made available in the most cost-efficient way? How can maintenance and repair costs of assistive products be minimized? To what extent can universal design principles and technological standards help develop high-quality, low-cost solutions? Human resource development for the assistive technology sector is another critical area. Professionals in healthcare, vocational rehabilitation, education, and social work need knowledge about available assistive products, how to match them to individual needs, and their appropriate and efficient use. Technical expertise is also essential for developing new assistive products and improving existing ones. Consequently, there is a need to establish standards and training programs for professionals in the assistive technology field. The focus and content of such programs are not self-evident. Research questions include: What competencies are essential for assistive technology professionals, and how can these capabilities be optimally developed? What are the cost-efficient opportunities to educate professionals at various levels of expertise, from basic knowledge to high-level expertise? How can information about available solutions be disseminated to professionals involved in service provision and others providing services for individuals with impairments? How can users or user groups be engaged in addressing the global shortage of assistive technology personnel? Is it possible to develop a standardized curriculum for professionals involved in assistive product provision? Standards and methodologies for assessing assistive technology needs and unmet needs are essential. The demand for assistive technology in a given country depends on numerous interrelated factors, such as available resources, economic conditions, the natural environment, population composition, and more. Tools and instruments are needed to analyze these factors and identify potential policies and actions to improve access to and optimal use of assistive products. These tools are required at various levels, including national, regional, and local governments, service providers, and individuals with disabilities. Research questions include: How can accurate data about the prevalence of impairments or disabilities be collected and used in a standardized, valid, and reliable way to enable effective planning and operation by governments and service providers? How can the individual needs of people with impairments or disabilities be assessed and matched to the most appropriate assistive technology solutions? What are the essential components of assistive technology needs assessment tools? How can coverage and user satisfaction rates be mapped? How can the global assistive technology landscape be mapped? Two general guiding principles emerged during the GATE Research Group consensus meeting. First, user involvement is essential in all aspects of research, policy development, system design, and service provision. Second, an environmental approach to functioning should be adopted instead of a traditional medical model. These principles should guide all related research priorities and may themselves require specific research to operationalize. The global priority research agenda invites all stakeholders to initiate or support research addressing identified global priority research questions. By doing so, they will help bridge the gap between assistive technology needs and unmet needs and close the divide between those who can access assistive technology based on wealth rather than actual need. The agenda is broad, and within each thematic area, numerous relevant research questions can be addressed. Researchers and research groups are encouraged to adapt these questions to their specific priorities and needs. It is hoped that research in assistive technology will converge toward the main thematic areas proposed in this document. The agenda is not only socially relevant but also scientifically challenging, with a lack of quality research and evidence in many thematic areas requiring the development of new methodologies. Researchers, professional organizations, and scientific bodies in the field of assistive technology are encouraged to collaborate internationally to stimulate and execute research as described in this agenda. Finally, the agenda presents significant opportunities for industry, with a vast market potential for developing and producing the right products at affordable costs. The GATE Research Group envisions innovative collaborations to implement this global priority assistive technology research agenda and bring much-needed assistive products and services to those in need.
